body.title: The Vineyards Above Manarola
body.subtitle: A winemaker's year in the terraced vineyards that have shaped these cliffs for a thousand years

body.quote: You don't grow wine here. You negotiate with stone, with slope, with the sea wind. The vines agree to stay if you tend them every single day.
body.leftContent:
Marco Capellini is telling me this while we stand in his family's vineyard, seven hundred meters above the port of Manarola, on a terrace held in place by a dry stone wall that his great-great-grandfather built in 1887. The wall is a meter thick, fitted without mortar, and it has not moved.

These are the vineyards that made Cinque Terre long before the walking path did. Terraces stacked impossibly up the coastal cliffs, each one defended against gravity and weather by muretti a secco — those patient walls of fitted stone that hold the whole improbable enterprise together. This is where Bosco and Albarola and Vermentino have grown for centuries, and where Sciacchetrà, the region's amber dessert wine, has been pressed and aged in damp stone cantinas since medieval times.
body.rightContent:
But Marco doesn't talk about medieval times. He talks about this year: what the spring rain did to the flowering, whether the August heat came too early, if the October harvest will start before or after the sea storms arrive. Wine here is not romantic. It's a discipline of attention.

I've known Marco since we were children — our families' terraces share a wall near the sanctuary of Nostra Signora della Salute — and I've watched him carry the same pruning shears his grandfather carried, walk the same hundred and thirty-seven steps up from the train tracks every morning before dawn. So when he offered to let me follow his year in the vines, I said yes immediately. Not because I wanted to write about wine, but because I wanted to understand what it means to keep faith with a place this demanding.

body.markdown: March is cold work. The vines are still bare sticks, and Marco moves through them with secateurs, cutting back last year's growth to just two or three buds per cane. Each cut is a small act of prophecy — you're deciding which wood will fruit in September, which branches will catch the sun. Get it wrong and you lose half the harvest. There's no mulling it over. The vine tells you where to cut if you know how to look.

By April the terraces start to green. Tiny leaves unfold, and the whole cliff face softens. This is when Marco worries most. A late frost, a week of heavy rain during flowering, and the year is compromised before it begins. He watches the weather like a man waiting for news. On clear mornings, he walks the rows checking for mold, for the first signs of peronospora — downy mildew — which loves the humidity that rises from the sea. Everything he does now is preparation for battles he'll fight in summer.

The work is relentless and small-scale. There are no tractors here, no machines wider than a wheelbarrow. Everything moves on the trenino — the little monorail track that clings to the slope, carrying baskets and tools and people up and down the gradient. You learn to carry what you need and nothing more. You learn to count your steps. You learn that this landscape was never meant to be easy.

July is when the grapes start to form, tight green clusters hiding under the leaf canopy. Marco thins them ruthlessly — cutting away half the bunches so the remaining fruit concentrates its sugars. It feels like waste until you taste what those fewer clusters become: dense, complex, bright with the minerals the vines pull from schist and limestone. Bosco, which makes up most of his vineyard, is a late-ripening variety that needs this kind of focus. It won't be rushed.

By August the heat is serious. The sun hits the terraces straight-on, no shade, just stone and vine and the white glare off the Ligurian Sea below. This is Vermentino weather — the variety loves it, ripens fast, keeps its acidity even when the thermometer pushes thirty-five degrees. Marco walks the rows in the early morning and again at dusk, checking the fruit, tasting for the shift from tart to ripe. You can't rely on dates here. The grapes tell you when they're ready, and every year is different.

There's a rhythm to the summer work that looks almost meditative from a distance: tie back the canes, trim the canopy for airflow, watch for wasps and wild boar. But the repetition isn't peaceful. It's a kind of sustained noticing, a refusal to let anything slip past your attention. This is what Marco means when he says you negotiate with the vines. You can't control the weather or the slope or the sea wind. You can only respond, every day, to what the vineyard asks of you.

body.alt: Hands holding fresh white grapes during vendemmia harvest in Cinque Terre vineyards
body.caption: White grapes at harvest — each cluster tasted and picked at exactly the right moment. Photo by Maël BALLAND on Unsplash

body.markdown: Harvest starts in late September, sometimes early October if the season has been cool. Marco picks section by section, variety by variety, never rushing, always waiting for the exact day when the sugar and acid and flavor are balanced. For the table wine — the white blend that most people drink with seafood — he picks Vermentino first, then Bosco, then Albarola. Each harvest happens over two or three days, carried down the mountain in plastic crates loaded onto the trenino, twenty kilos at a time.

But for the Sciacchetrà, he waits longer. Another three weeks, sometimes four, letting the grapes shrivel and concentrate on the vine. The clusters get smaller, denser, sticky with sugar. Some of them start to raisin. This is the fruit that becomes the region's legendary dessert wine — amber, complex, tasting of dried apricot and honey and something faintly bitter, like almond skin. It's a wine that takes patience to make and patience to drink. You don't pour it for tourists in a hurry.

body.quote: I remember my first vendemmia — I was eight, and my grandmother handed me a pair of scissors and told me to cut only the clusters that looked 'ready.' I had no idea what that meant. She laughed and said I'd know by the end of the day. She was right. Your hands learn the weight of a ripe bunch, the way it gives when you touch it. Your eyes learn the color shift from green-gold to amber. It's a knowledge that lives in the body, not the head. Marco has that knowledge in a way I never will. But I understand why he keeps coming back to these terraces, year after year. Some things you tend not because they're easy, but because they're yours.
body.author: Giulia Rossi

body.markdown: By November the vines are bare again, and the terraces fall quiet. The harvest is in the cellar, fermenting slowly in stainless steel and old chestnut barrels. This is when Marco finally exhales. The wine will take its time now — months for the table whites, years for the Sciacchetrà, which ages in small barrels and develops that characteristic oxidative note, that warm complexity that sommeliers describe as 'haunting' and Marco just calls 'right.'

December and January are for maintenance. Rebuilding sections of wall that shifted during autumn rains. Clearing brush. Oiling tools. Walking the terraces to see how the land weathered the year. The vineyard never stops asking for attention, even when there's no fruit on the vine. This is the part that visitors don't see — the slow, unglamorous work of keeping an ancient system intact. But it's the part that makes everything else possible.

If you want to understand these vineyards, taste the Sciacchetrà. Not at a restaurant, where it's served in tiny pours to tourists who aren't sure what to make of it. Taste it in a cantina, from a producer who makes maybe five hundred bottles a year, who can tell you which terrace the grapes came from and what the weather was like that October.

The wine is made from the same grapes as the table whites — mostly Bosco, with some Albarola and Vermentino — but left to concentrate on the vine until they're almost raisins. After harvest, the grapes are laid out to dry further, sometimes for weeks, before pressing. The fermentation is slow, sometimes stopping and starting over months. The result is a wine with fifteen or sixteen percent alcohol, sweet but not cloying, with a tannic grip and an acidity that keeps it from tipping into dessert-wine territory. It's the kind of wine you sip after dinner with a piece of dark chocolate or a wedge of aged pecorino. It asks you to slow down.

Marco's Sciacchetrà is three years old before he releases it, and even then he'll tell you it could use more time. Traditionalists say five years minimum, ten if you can wait. I've tasted twenty-year-old bottles that were still vibrant, still unfolding. This is not wine made for the market. It's wine made because the place demands it, because the tradition asks you to keep it alive, because your grandfather did it and his grandfather before him.

body.title: The Discipline of Place
body.content:
When I ask Marco why he does this — why he spends his life on these punishing slopes when he could make easier wine elsewhere — he looks at me like the question doesn't parse. 'This is the vineyard,' he says. 'It's not mine. I'm just the one taking care of it right now.'

That's the thing about these terraces. They were here before any of us, and they'll be here after. The walls were built by people whose names we've forgotten, and they're maintained by people whose children might not continue the work. But the vineyard persists because enough people, in each generation, decide it matters. Not because it's profitable — it barely is. Not because it's easy — it's absolutely not. But because some kinds of knowledge are worth preserving, even when they cost you everything.

The wine is just the evidence. What you're really tasting is the attention.
